article.title: Firefox 159 Enables Scroll-Driven Animations by Default and Adds Scoped Custom Element Registries; web.dev Lists Both as Baseline Newly Available
article.summary: Firefox 159, released October 27, 2026, enables scroll-driven animations by default and adds scoped custom element registries, which web.dev lists as Baseline Newly available; legacy masonry syntax is removed.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Firefox 159 was released on October 27, 2026, according to [MDN's release notes for developers](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Mozilla/Firefox/Releases/159). The release enables scroll-driven animations by default and adds support for scoped custom element registries, both listed in the same notes. In its ["New to the web platform in October" post](https://web.dev/blog/web-platform-10-2026), published October 29, 2026, web.dev lists both features as Baseline Newly available.

## Scroll-driven animations

MDN says that "Scroll-driven animations are now enabled by default" in Firefox 159 and describes them as a way to animate property values along a scroll-based timeline rather than along the default time-based document timeline. The [Firefox release notes](https://www.firefox.com/en-US/firefox/159.0/releasenotes/) say the change adds the `animation-timeline`, `scroll-timeline`, `view-timeline` and `animation-range` properties and the `ScrollTimeline` and `ViewTimeline` interfaces.

web.dev writes: "With support in Chrome, Safari, and now Firefox 159, scroll-driven animations are Baseline Newly available." The post's browser-support table for the feature lists Chrome 115, Edge 115, Firefox 159 and Safari 26. The WebKit blog's [Safari 26.0 feature post](https://webkit.org/blog/17333/webkit-features-in-safari-26-0/), dated Sep 15, 2025, names scroll-driven animations among the features arriving in that release.

In a [DEV Community post](https://dev.to/richicodes/scroll-driven-animations-are-baseline-at-last-3c8g) dated Nov 4, author richi.codes says the demo checks `CSS.supports('animation-timeline: scroll()')` and falls back to a JavaScript scroll listener and an `IntersectionObserver` when the check fails. The author also reports that an `overflow: hidden` track made `scroll(nearest)` find the track instead of the panel, because `hidden` turns an element into a scroll container, and that switching to `overflow: clip` fixed it.

## Scoped custom element registries

According to MDN, scoped custom element registries let a shadow tree create an independent `CustomElementRegistry` whose definitions only apply to that specific DOM subtree, which can avoid collisions where multiple web components declare elements with the same name. MDN adds that the `customElementRegistry` property can be used on `Document`, `Element` and `ShadowRoot`, and that the `CustomElementRegistry()` constructor creates a new registry object for scoped usage. The Herald's [earlier Firefox 156 coverage](/article/2026-09/30-firefox-156-ships-scheduleryield-priority-inheritance-text-box-trim-fixes-and-a-45-faster-pdf-viewer-startup) noted that, per MDN's Firefox 156 notes, scoped custom element registries were then disabled by default and had to be enabled through `about:config`.

web.dev describes the problem this addresses: "Previously, all custom elements had to be registered in a single global window.customElements registry, which could cause naming collisions when combining components from different libraries or teams." It adds: "With support across Chrome, Safari, and Firefox 159, scoped custom element registries are now Baseline Newly available." Its support table lists Chrome 146, Edge 146, Firefox 159 and Safari 26.

A [Chrome for Developers blog post](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/scoped-registries) published March 9, 2026, says scoped custom element registries are "now available by default from Edge and Chrome 146, as well as other Chromium-based browsers." A [DEV Community post](https://dev.to/iamprincejkc/stop-prefixing-every-custom-element-name-scoped-registries-are-baseline-1lo2) by an author identified as JKC, dated Nov 7, says Safari 26.0 shipped the feature first and that Safari 26.4 added upgrading elements in `initialize()` plus fixes around `null` registries. The same author reports that `document.createElement()` still uses the global registry by default and that `initialize()` is first come, first served: after calling it twice on one shadow root in Chrome, the root kept the first registry.

## Other changes in the release

MDN lists a removal alongside the additions: the legacy masonry layout syntax, meaning the `masonry` value of `grid-template-columns` and `grid-template-rows` and the `masonry-auto-flow` property. MDN says that syntax was only enabled by default in Nightly, behind a preference, and that it is superseded by grid lanes layout, which uses the `grid-lanes` and `inline-grid-lanes` values of the `display` property.

Among other developer-facing items, MDN says HTML Sanitizer API methods such as `Element.setHTML()` now remove unwanted elements and attributes as the markup is parsed rather than afterwards. The Firefox release notes add that the Web Console now allows `let`, `const` and `class` variables to be declared again so a snippet can be edited and re-run, and that, on compatible devices, WebGL supports the `EXT_clip_control` and `EXT_texture_mirror_clamp_to_edge` extensions while WebGL 2 supports `EXT_texture_norm16`.

## What the sources do not say

The DEV Community post on scroll-driven animations notes that Baseline "newly available" means every engine ships a feature, not that every user has updated, and advises keeping a fallback for a while. None of the sources cited here reports adoption figures for either feature or for Firefox 159.
